title: Do Private Firms Invest Differently than Public Firms? Taking Cues from the Natural Gas Industry
research_question: How does a firm's listing status (public versus private) affect its investment behavior in response to changes in investment opportunities? Specifically, do private and public firms differ in how they respond to shifts in output prices and to the emergence of new, capital-intensive growth opportunities, and does access to external capital help explain any such differences?
data_description: The primary data source is Schlumberger's Smith International Rig Count, which provides weekly information on every rig actively drilling a natural gas well in the United States from 1997 to 2012, including location, well type, operator, and timing. The authors hand-classify operators as public, private, or subsidiaries via Lexis Nexis and internet searches. The unit of observation is a firm-year (or firm-county-year) covering 74,670 individual drilling projects, yielding 1,813 private firm-years (380 unique firms) and 569 public firm-years (92 unique firms) over 2000–2012. Key variables include the number of new wells drilled (investment), wells drilled over the prior three years (capital stock), wellhead natural gas prices from the EIA, county-level shale discoveries, acreage/ownership data from the Oklahoma Corporation Commission, IPO prospectuses, and SDC asset-sale transaction data matched with CRSP returns.
institutional_context: The U.S. onshore natural gas industry provides an unusually clean setting for comparing public and private firms. Output is a homogeneous, competitively priced commodity, drilling technology is largely contracted out so all firms have similar access, and per-well costs do not vary systematically with firm size. This means public and private firms operating in the same area face essentially the same project-level revenues, costs, and technology. Two sources of variation in investment opportunities are exploited: fluctuations in wellhead natural gas prices over 2000–2012, and the staggered emergence of commercially viable shale gas plays beginning in 2003, when hydraulic fracturing combined with horizontal drilling unlocked shale reserves across 102 counties in six states. Shale wells require roughly $6.7–$9.5 million each, versus under $1 million for conventional wells, making shale a capital-intensive growth opportunity relative to traditional drilling.
